paper.title: Public Pensions and Private Savings
paper.code_data_availability: Replication package: Garcia-Miralles, Esteban, and Jonathan Leganza. …

registers.role: sample frame; treatment assignment (exact date of birth relative to the January 1, 1954, cutoff); controls (gender, marital status in 2010, region of residence in 2010); linkage via unique personal identifiers

outcomes: pretax labor market earnings (income on which the 8 percent labor market tax is paid), annual VERP benefit payments, and the third-party reported year-end balances used to build the savings flows
variables_mentioned: pretax earnings (income subject to the 8 percent labor market tax)

registers.role: outcomes: contributions to employer-sponsored retirement plans, to personal retirement plans and to Roth-style plans, and annuitized distributions from retirement accounts

registers.name_in_paper: labor market registers: 'IDA ansaettelser (IDAN, Employment, 1985-2018)' (Statistics Denmark 2022c)
registers.role: employer-employee linkage: assigning individuals to workplaces in 2010 in order to infer firm default contribution rates as the firm median contribution rate

registers.name_in_paper: monthly eIncome register: 'Detaljeret loenmodtagerdata fra e-indkomst (BFL, eIncome Employee, 2008-2017)' (Statistics Denmark 2022b)
registers.role: monthly employment and earnings information used to define monthly retirement ages (last month with positive earnings before they permanently fall to zero) and for the bunching analysis in Figure 4
variables_mentioned: monthly earnings reported by firms to the tax authorities

registers.name_in_paper: monthly eIncome register: 'Ikke loenmodtagerdata fra e-indkomst (ILME, eIncome Non-employee, 2008-2017)' (Statistics Denmark 2022d)
registers.role: monthly information on government transfers for all individuals, used to define monthly VERP claiming ages for the bunching analysis in Figure 4
variables_mentioned: pension benefits paid by the government to all recipients

registers.name_in_paper: property appraisals computed by the Danish tax authorities (SKAT), accessed through the register data
registers.role: outcome: year-end model-based appraisal values of properties, differenced to give the flow of property wealth

linkages: Individuals linked across population and labor market registers by unique personal identifiers to build an annual panel for the entire Danish population, 1985-2018
Individuals linked to the complementary monthly eIncome datasets (2008-2017) to track exits from the labor force and benefit claiming at monthly frequency
Individuals over 18 assigned to workplaces (firms) in 2010 so that a firm default contribution rate can be inferred as the median contribution rate among co-workers at the same firm

sample.universe: The entire population of Denmark, 1985-2018, in annual administrative register data
sample.unit_of_observation: individual (person-year panel; the main RD regressions are cross-sectional at the individual level, with outcomes averaged, taken in a single year, or cumulated)
selection_rules: Keep only Danes born within six months of the cutoff date, January 1, 1954
Keep only individuals who made participatory contributions to the VERP scheme in at least 70 percent of the preannouncement years 2001-2010
Balance the sample between 2006 and 2018: exclude individuals who are not in the data for all of these years
Exclude the self-employed, defined during the preannouncement period, who face different VERP rules

For the RD regressions, keep those born within 74 days of the cutoff - the Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in the first critical year, 2014, used throughout to hold the underlying sample constant
For the firm default rate exercises, keep those for whom a 2010 workplace (and hence default contribution rate) can be defined: 14,869 individuals, about 94 percent of the RD sample
sample.period: Register data 1985-2018; the analysis window is 2011-2018 (ages 57-64) with 2008-2010 used as a placebo pre-period and 2010 for summary statistics and the firm default proxy
sample.n_observations: 15,789 individuals in the RD estimation sample (one observation per individual per specification); 40,042 in the wider analysis sample; 6,596 frequent and 9,193 infrequent previous contributors to personal plans; 14,869 with an inferable firm default rate
sample.n_individuals: 15,789 (RD estimation sample); 40,042 (analysis sample); 57,178 (unrestricted sample without the VERP participation requirement)

construction_notes: Contributions to retirement accounts and pretax earnings are winsorized by year at the ninety-fifth percentile; the stock-based savings variables (bank accounts, stock market accounts, property wealth, liabilities), which are not bounded below by zero, are winsorized at the fifth and ninety-fifth percentile in each year
A robustness exercise winsorizes all outcomes more aggressively at the tenth and ninetieth percentiles, following Chetty et al. (2014) (online Appendix Table A.6)
Savings flows for bank accounts, stock market accounts, property wealth and liabilities are constructed as the year-end balance in year t minus the year-end balance in year t-1

Total (net) retirement savings = contributions to all retirement accounts minus distributions from retirement accounts; total nonretirement savings = changes in bank accounts + changes in stock market accounts + changes in property values - changes in liabilities; total savings = the sum of the two
All monetary values are deflated to 2010 levels and converted from Danish kroner to US dollars at the 2010 rate of approximately 5.56 kr. to $1

Monthly retirement age is an absorbing-state measure: the age in the last month during which earnings are positive before permanently falling to zero; monthly claiming age is the age upon initial receipt of VERP benefits

Firm default contribution rates are proxied by the median contribution rate (contributions to employer plans divided by earnings) among all individuals over 18 assigned to the same workplace in 2010; predicted contributions are current earnings times that 2010 rate

Liabilities cover the year-end value of all debts except private debt, including bank, credit card and mortgage debt; the data omit cash outside bank accounts, private debt to individuals and the value of consumer durables
Bandwidth 74 days with triangular weights throughout the main analysis; sensitivity shown from 28 to 180 days

claims.statement: Being born on or after the January 1, 1954, cutoff, and so facing pension eligibility ages six months higher, had no statistically distinguishable effect on average earnings (RD estimate 648, SE (873)), measured over average of the annual outcome over the three-year anticipation period 2011-2013 (ages 57-59).

treatment.label: Increase in pension eligibility ages due to the 2011 Danish reform (indicator for being born on or after the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff)

register_source.value: BEF (Statistics Denmark 2022a, 'Befolkningen (BEF, Population Demographics, 1985-2018)'): exact date of birth

definition.value: 1[x_i >= c], where x_i is exact date of birth and c = January 1, 1954. Those born on or after the cutoff learn in 2011, at age 57, that their early retirement age, incentivized retirement age and full retirement age have each risen by six months, to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5; those born just before keep 60, 62 and 65. A sharp, six-month increase in all three public pension eligibility ages; benefit amounts and means-testing rules are unchanged for these cohorts.

timing.value: Announced May 2011, when the analysis sample is age 57; implemented in 2014, when the sample reaches age 60. Treatment status is fixed at birth.

register_source.value: IND (Statistics Denmark 2022e, 'Indkomst (IND, Income, 1985-2018)'); the paper names the register but not the variable

definition.value: Annual pretax labor market earnings, defined as the amount of income on which individuals pay an 8 percent labor market tax; winsorized by year at the ninety-fifth percentile and deflated to 2010 US dollars. The paper's main measure of labor supply. Construction window: average of the annual outcome over the three-year anticipation period 2011-2013 (ages 57-59).

timing.value: Measured over average of the annual outcome over the three-year anticipation period 2011-2013 (ages 57-59). The reform was announced in May 2011 (sample age 57) and implemented in 2014 (sample age 60).

units.value: 2010 US dollars per year (average annual amount over 2011-2013)

estimand.target_population: VERP participants born right around (within 74 days of) the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff; the paper describes beta as the average impact of the six-month increase in pension eligibility ages for those born right around the cutoff
estimand.time_horizon: outcomes averaged over the three-year anticipation period 2011 to 2013, i.e. years 0 to 2 after the May 2011 announcement and before the 2014 implementation (ages 57 to 59)
estimand.formal_query: lim_{x down to c} E[Y|X=x] - lim_{x up to c} E[Y|X=x], read as E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60.5/62.5/65.5)] - E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60/62/65)] for VERP participants with birth date at c = January 1, 1954

population.description: Danes born within 74 days of the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff who made participatory contributions to the VERP early retirement scheme in at least 70 percent of the preannouncement years 2001-2010, who are present in the data in every year 2006-2018, and who were not self-employed in the preannouncement period (the RD estimation sample of 15,789 individuals)
population.birth_cohorts: born within 74 days of January 1, 1954 (the baseline bandwidth); the wider analysis sample is those born within six months of January 1, 1954
subgroups_defined: treatment (born on or after January 1, 1954) versus control (born just before)
frequent versus infrequent previous contributors to personal retirement plans (contributed in two or three versus zero or one of the years 2008-2010)
individuals for whom a 2010 firm default contribution rate can be inferred (94 percent of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on VERP participation before the announcement (contributions in at least 70 percent of 2001-2010), on being in the data in all years 2006-2018 (i.e. alive and resident in Denmark), on not being self-employed in the preannouncement period, and on being born within 74 days of the cutoff - the Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for 2014 labor market earnings.

identification.source_of_variation: The May 2011 Danish reform on later retirement, which raised the early retirement age, the incentivized retirement age and the full retirement age by six months - from 60, 62 and 65 to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5 - for everyone born on or after January 1, 1954, and left them unchanged for those born one day earlier. The first of the reform's stepwise birth-date discontinuities, which the authors call the cleanest quasi-experiment it creates.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). The order of the polynomial is not varied.

threats_discussed: Manipulation of the running variable (argued impossible: birth date is fixed decades before the announcement; density test p-value 0.125)
Some other policy changing discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, cutoff, in particular school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017)
Differential attrition by birth date (death or emigration), since the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 and therefore conditions on being alive and in Denmark
Capital gains from selling property making financial account flows hard to interpret (addressed by excluding individuals with real estate transactions, online Appendix Table A.5)
The 2012 option for VERP members to opt out of the scheme, which could change participation at the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.9 finds no response)
Lack of statistical precision over the anticipation period, which prevents ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes
Lack of awareness of the reform during the anticipation period (argued unlikely: the reform was well publicized; Google search intensity for 'efterloen' spikes, online Appendix Figure A.9)
Inability to respond in anticipation because of low liquid assets ('hand-to-mouth' behaviour), probed on the subsample of previous users of personal retirement plans (online Appendix Table A.10)
robustness_checks: Bandwidths varied from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4, A.5, A.6; right-hand panels of Figure 8)
Dropping triangular weights and excluding control variables (online Appendix Table A.4)
More aggressive winsorization at the tenth and ninetieth percentiles, following Chetty et al. (2014) (online Appendix Table A.6)
Placebo time period: RD estimated over the preannouncement years 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7)
Placebo cutoffs at birth dates around the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8)
Placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 birth cohorts at their critical ages 60 and 62 (online Appendix Table A.8)
Excluding individuals with real estate transactions from the anticipation-period analysis (online Appendix Table A.5)
Density test of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1; Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma 2019 p-value 0.125)
RD on each predetermined control variable as an outcome (online Appendix Table A.2)
RD on the likelihood of making participatory VERP contributions, to check for a participation response (online Appendix Table A.9)
unresolved_confounders: School-starting-age discontinuities for those born in January versus December (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017): the authors argue from two placebo exercises that this is unlikely to matter but do not rule it out directly
Differential attrition by birth date induced by the reform, since the sample is balanced on being alive and in Denmark; investigated only indirectly
Over the anticipation period, standard errors that 'prevent us from ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes'

In the Table 7 exercise, the difference between actual and predicted contributions is not explained: it could reflect genuine savings responses or workers who previously contributed above their default rate continuing to do so

estimator.value: Sharp regression discontinuity in date of birth, estimated by weighted least squares with separate linear polynomials in the running variable on either side of the cutoff, triangular weights and a 74-day bandwidth (equation 6); robust standard errors

estimation.specification: Equation (6): y_i = alpha + beta*1[x_i >= c] + gamma*(x_i - c) + delta*1[x_i >= c]*(x_i - c) + Z_i theta + eps_i, with x_i = date of birth, c = January 1, 1954, Z_i = gender, married in 2010 and region-of-residence dummies; triangular weights; bandwidth 74 days.
controls: dummy for gender
dummy for being married in the preannouncement year 2010
dummies for the five preannouncement-year administrative regions of residence (2010)
estimation.weights: triangular weights in the running variable (date of birth), bandwidth 74 days

source_table.value: Table 2, Panel A. Labor supply, 'Average earnings' row, column (1) (RD estimate); column (2) gives the mean

adjustment_set.label: Date of birth (running variable), entered as separate linear polynomials on either side of the cutoff
Dummy for gender
Dummy for being married in the preannouncement year 2010
Dummies for the five preannouncement-year administrative regions of residence

mediators_claimed: Extended employment: the new eligibility ages induce treated individuals to work roughly six months longer, raising earnings and mechanically the flow of contributions
ambiguities: The paper stresses that the anticipation-period estimates lack precision: 'our standard errors prevent us from ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes', and a back-of-the-envelope calculation implies an expected decline of about $220 per year in total savings, which the confidence interval does not exclude.

value.as_printed: y_i = alpha + beta * 1[x_i >= c] + gamma * (x_i - c) + delta * 1[x_i >= c] * (x_i - c) + Z_i theta + epsilon_i

index_sets.over: individuals in the RD estimation sample

value.normalisation: The running variable is centred at the cutoff c = January 1, 1954; the reference group is those born just before the cutoff, who keep eligibility ages 60, 62 and 65. Triangular weights and a bandwidth of 74 days on either side. All monetary outcomes are deflated to 2010 levels and converted from Danish kroner to US dollars (about 5.56 kr. to $1).

theory_referenced: Life cycle model of consumption with an endogenous retirement decision (Laitner and Silverman 2007; Hurd, Michaud, and Rohwedder 2012)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: We note that recent work that focuses on labor supply and earnings in the context of pension reform also finds little support for forward-looking responses (Gelber, Isen, and Song 2016 and Haller 2019).

anchor_quote.text: We find no evidence of anticipatory savings responses, although we show that our estimates over this period suffer from a lack of statistical precision.

definition.value: 1[x_i >= c], where x_i is exact date of birth and c = January 1, 1954. Those born on or after the cutoff learn in 2011, at age 57, that their early retirement age, incentivized retirement age and full retirement age have each risen by six months, to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5; those born just before keep 60, 62 and 65. A sharp, six-month increase in all three public pension eligibility ages; benefit amounts and means-testing rules are unchanged for these cohorts.

timing.value: Announced May 2011, when the analysis sample is age 57; implemented in 2014, when the sample reaches age 60. Treatment status is fixed at birth.

definition.value: Annual contributions to personal defined-contribution retirement accounts (analogous to US IRAs), a flow variable; contributing to these plans is completely voluntary. timing.value: Measured over average of the annual outcome over the three-year anticipation period 2011-2013 (ages 57-59). The reform was announced in May 2011 (sample age 57) and implemented in 2014 (sample age 60).

estimand.target_population: VERP participants born right around (within 74 days of) the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff; the paper describes beta as the average impact of the six-month increase in pension eligibility ages for those born right around the cutoff
estimand.time_horizon: outcomes averaged over the three-year anticipation period 2011 to 2013, i.e. years 0 to 2 after the May 2011 announcement and before the 2014 implementation (ages 57 to 59)
estimand.formal_query: lim_{x down to c} E[Y|X=x] - lim_{x up to c} E[Y|X=x], read as E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60.5/62.5/65.5)] - E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60/62/65)] for VERP participants with birth date at c = January 1, 1954

population.description: Danes born within 74 days of the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff who made participatory contributions to the VERP early retirement scheme in at least 70 percent of the preannouncement years 2001-2010, who are present in the data in every year 2006-2018, and who were not self-employed in the preannouncement period (the RD estimation sample of 15,789 individuals)
population.birth_cohorts: born within 74 days of January 1, 1954 (the baseline bandwidth); the wider analysis sample is those born within six months of January 1, 1954
subgroups_defined: treatment (born on or after January 1, 1954) versus control (born just before)
frequent versus infrequent previous contributors to personal retirement plans (contributed in two or three versus zero or one of the years 2008-2010)
individuals for whom a 2010 firm default contribution rate can be inferred (94 percent of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on VERP participation before the announcement (contributions in at least 70 percent of 2001-2010), on being in the data in all years 2006-2018 (i.e. alive and resident in Denmark), on not being self-employed in the preannouncement period, and on being born within 74 days of the cutoff - the Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for 2014 labor market earnings.

identification.source_of_variation: The May 2011 Danish reform on later retirement, which raised the early retirement age, the incentivized retirement age and the full retirement age by six months - from 60, 62 and 65 to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5 - for everyone born on or after January 1, 1954, and left them unchanged for those born one day earlier. The first of the reform's stepwise birth-date discontinuities, which the authors call the cleanest quasi-experiment it creates.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). The order of the polynomial is not varied.

threats_discussed: Manipulation of the running variable (argued impossible: birth date is fixed decades before the announcement; density test p-value 0.125)

Capital gains from selling property making financial account flows hard to interpret (addressed by excluding individuals with real estate transactions, online Appendix Table A.5)
The 2012 option for VERP members to opt out of the scheme, which could change participation at the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.9 finds no response)
Lack of statistical precision over the anticipation period, which prevents ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes

ambiguities: The paper's life cycle benchmark predicts a negative effect on savings in this period (anticipation: savings fall; reform-induced extended employment: savings rise), which is why prediction_risk is recorded as 'direction'.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days

ambiguities: The paper's life cycle benchmark predicts a negative effect on savings in this period (anticipation: savings fall; reform-induced extended employment: savings rise), which is why prediction_risk is recorded as 'direction'.

The paper stresses that the anticipation-period estimates lack precision: 'our standard errors prevent us from ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes', and a back-of-the-envelope calculation implies an expected decline of about $220 per year in total savings, which the confidence interval does not exclude.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). threats_discussed: Manipulation of the running variable (argued impossible: birth date is fixed decades before the announcement; density test p-value 0.125)

Differential attrition by birth date (death or emigration), since the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 and therefore conditions on being alive and in Denmark
Capital gains from selling property making financial account flows hard to interpret (addressed by excluding individuals with real estate transactions, online Appendix Table A.5)
The 2012 option for VERP members to opt out of the scheme, which could change participation at the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.9 finds no response)
Lack of statistical precision over the anticipation period, which prevents ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes

definition.value: 1[x_i >= c], where x_i is exact date of birth and c = January 1, 1954. key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). treatment.label: Increase in pension eligibility ages due to the 2011 Danish reform (indicator for being born on or after the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff)

register_source.value: BEF (Statistics Denmark 2022a, 'Befolkningen (BEF, Population Demographics, 1985-2018)'): exact date of birth

definition.value: 1[x_i >= c], where x_i is exact date of birth and c = January 1, 1954. Those born on or after the cutoff learn in 2011, at age 57, that their early retirement age, incentivized retirement age and full retirement age have each risen by six months, to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5; those born just before keep 60, 62 and 65. A sharp, six-month increase in all three public pension eligibility ages; benefit amounts and means-testing rules are unchanged for these cohorts.

timing.value: Announced May 2011, when the analysis sample is age 57; implemented in 2014, when the sample reaches age 60. Treatment status is fixed at birth.

register_source.value: IND (Statistics Denmark 2022e, 'Indkomst (IND, Income, 1985-2018)'); the paper names the register but not the variable

definition.value: Annual pretax labor market earnings, defined as the amount of income on which individuals pay an 8 percent labor market tax; winsorized by year at the ninety-fifth percentile and deflated to 2010 US dollars. The paper's main measure of labor supply. Construction window: calendar year 2017, a noncritical year, when the sample is age 63.

timing.value: Measured over calendar year 2017, a noncritical year, when the sample is age 63. The reform was announced in May 2011 (sample age 57) and implemented in 2014 (sample age 60).

estimand.target_population: VERP participants born right around (within 74 days of) the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff; the paper describes beta as the average impact of the six-month increase in pension eligibility ages for those born right around the cutoff
estimand.time_horizon: calendar year 2017, a noncritical year (age 63), six years after the May 2011 announcement
estimand.formal_query: lim_{x down to c} E[Y|X=x] - lim_{x up to c} E[Y|X=x], read as E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60.5/62.5/65.5)] - E[Y|do(eligibility ages 60/62/65)] for VERP participants with birth date at c = January 1, 1954

population.description: Danes born within 74 days of the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff who made participatory contributions to the VERP early retirement scheme in at least 70 percent of the preannouncement years 2001-2010, who are present in the data in every year 2006-2018, and who were not self-employed in the preannouncement period (the RD estimation sample of 15,789 individuals)
population.birth_cohorts: born within 74 days of January 1, 1954 (the baseline bandwidth); the wider analysis sample is those born within six months of January 1, 1954
subgroups_defined: treatment (born on or after January 1, 1954) versus control (born just before)
frequent versus infrequent previous contributors to personal retirement plans (contributed in two or three versus zero or one of the years 2008-2010)
individuals for whom a 2010 firm default contribution rate can be inferred (94 percent of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on VERP participation before the announcement (contributions in at least 70 percent of 2001-2010), on being in the data in all years 2006-2018 (i.e. alive and resident in Denmark), on not being self-employed in the preannouncement period, and on being born within 74 days of the cutoff - the Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for 2014 labor market earnings.

identification.source_of_variation: The May 2011 Danish reform on later retirement, which raised the early retirement age, the incentivized retirement age and the full retirement age by six months - from 60, 62 and 65 to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5 - for everyone born on or after January 1, 1954, and left them unchanged for those born one day earlier. The first of the reform's stepwise birth-date discontinuities, which the authors call the cleanest quasi-experiment it creates.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). The order of the polynomial is not varied.

threats_discussed: Manipulation of the running variable (argued impossible: birth date is fixed decades before the announcement; density test p-value 0.125)
Some other policy changing discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, cutoff, in particular school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017)
Differential attrition by birth date (death or emigration), since the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 and therefore conditions on being alive and in Denmark
Capital gains from selling property making financial account flows hard to interpret (addressed by excluding individuals with real estate transactions, online Appendix Table A.5)
The 2012 option for VERP members to opt out of the scheme, which could change participation at the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.9 finds no response)
Lack of statistical precision over the anticipation period, which prevents ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes
Lack of awareness of the reform during the anticipation period (argued unlikely: the reform was well publicized; Google search intensity for 'efterloen' spikes, online Appendix Figure A.9)
Inability to respond in anticipation because of low liquid assets ('hand-to-mouth' behaviour), probed on the subsample of previous users of personal retirement plans (online Appendix Table A.10)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). population.description: Danes born within 74 days of the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff who made participatory contributions to the VERP early retirement scheme in at least 70 percent of the preannouncement years 2001-2010, who are present in the data in every year 2006-2018, and who were not self-employed in the preannouncement period (the RD estimation sample of 15,789 individuals), restricted to the frequent-contributor subsample
population.birth_cohorts: born within 74 days of January 1, 1954 (the baseline bandwidth); the wider analysis sample is those born within six months of January 1, 1954
subgroups_defined: treatment (born on or after January 1, 1954) versus control (born just before)
frequent versus infrequent previous contributors to personal retirement plans (contributed in two or three versus zero or one of the years 2008-2010)
individuals for whom a 2010 firm default contribution rate can be inferred (94 percent of the sample)
population.selection: Conditioned on VERP participation before the announcement (contributions in at least 70 percent of 2001-2010), on being in the data in all years 2006-2018 (i.e. alive and resident in Denmark), on not being self-employed in the preannouncement period, and on being born within 74 days of the cutoff - the Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for 2014 labor market earnings.

identification.source_of_variation: The May 2011 Danish reform's six-month increase in pension eligibility ages for those born on or after January 1, 1954, estimated separately within subsamples defined by preannouncement use of personal retirement plans.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). The order of the polynomial is not varied.

threats_discussed: Manipulation of the running variable (argued impossible: birth date is fixed decades before the announcement; density test p-value 0.125)
Some other policy changing discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, cutoff, in particular school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017)
Differential attrition by birth date (death or emigration), since the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 and therefore conditions on being alive and in Denmark
Capital gains from selling property making financial account flows hard to interpret (addressed by excluding individuals with real estate transactions, online Appendix Table A.5)
The 2012 option for VERP members to opt out of the scheme, which could change participation at the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.9 finds no response)
Lack of statistical precision over the anticipation period, which prevents ruling out a priori plausible effect sizes
Lack of awareness of the reform during the anticipation period (argued unlikely: the reform was well publicized; Google search intensity for 'efterloen' spikes, online Appendix Figure A.9)
Inability to respond in anticipation because of low liquid assets ('hand-to-mouth' behaviour), probed on the subsample of previous users of personal retirement plans (online Appendix Table A.10)
robustness_checks: Bandwidths varied from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4, A.5, A.6; right-hand panels of Figure 8)
Dropping triangular weights and excluding control variables (online Appendix Table A.4)
More aggressive winsorization at the tenth and ninetieth percentiles, following Chetty et al. (2014) (online Appendix Table A.6)

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: RD continuity: in the absence of the policy-induced discontinuity in pension eligibility ages, outcome variables would have evolved smoothly in birth date through the January 1, 1954, cutoff; all other factors that could influence the outcome do so smoothly through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo RD over the preannouncement period 2008-2010 (online Appendix Table A.7, no statistically significant effects); placebo cutoffs away from the true cutoff (online Appendix Figures A.7, A.8); the entire analysis replicated at placebo January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts (online Appendix Table A.8); smoothness of the predetermined control variables through the cutoff (online Appendix Table A.2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: birth date cannot be manipulated in response to the reform, so the density of birth date is smooth through the cutoff
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued institutionally (birth date was determined decades before the 2011 announcement) and tested with a histogram plus local polynomial fit of the running variable (online Appendix Figure A.1) and the Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2019) density test at the baseline bandwidth, which yields a p-value of 0.125, so the null of a smooth density is not rejected.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the mixed mortality literature and from Nielsen (2019), who finds no mortality effect of early retirement in Denmark; investigated indirectly with the density test of the running variable. Not tested directly.

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). The order of the polynomial is not varied.

key_assumptions.assumption: The median contribution rate among workers at an individual's 2010 firm is a valid proxy for that firm's default contribution rate
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Chetty et al. (2014) and Fadlon, Laird, and Nielsen (2016); the authors concede measurement error (the median worker may contribute more than the default, and workers within a firm may be covered by different collective bargaining agreements) and show in Figure 9 panel A that the propensity to deviate from the inferred default did not differ by treatment group before the reform.

key_assumptions.assumption: No other policy or institutional rule changes discontinuously at the January 1, 1954, birth date cutoff and affects the outcome (the authors name school starting age as the candidate)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors are 'not aware of other reforms that specifically targeted this birth date discontinuity' and note that Danish education policy can create school-starting-age discontinuities for January versus December births (Landersoe, Nielsen, and Simonsen 2017); they offer two placebo exercises instead of a direct test - no discontinuities in preannouncement-period outcomes, and no discontinuities at January 1 cutoffs for the unaffected 1951 and 1952 cohorts at their critical ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential attrition by birth date: because the sample is balanced over 2006-2018 it is conditioned on being alive and in Denmark, and this selection must be unrelated to the outcome given birth date

key_assumptions.assumption: The conditional expectation of the outcome is well approximated by separate linear functions of birth date on either side of the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth of 74 days
key_assumptions.supported_by: The bandwidth is the Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) optimal bandwidth for labor market earnings in 2014 (74 days) and is held fixed throughout; sensitivity is shown for bandwidths from 28 to 180 days (online Appendix Figures A.4-A.6 and the right-hand panels of Figure 8). key_assumptions.assumption: The median contribution rate among workers at an individual's 2010 firm is a valid proxy for that firm's default contribution rate, so that earnings times that rate is what a passive worker would contribute
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Chetty et al. (2014) and Fadlon, Laird, and Nielsen (2016); measurement error is conceded; Figure 9 panel A shows the pre-reform distributions of deviations from the inferred default lie on top of one another for treatment and control.

key_assumptions.assumption: The difference between the actual and the predicted discontinuity can be read as the part of the response not explained by default rates
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors explicitly qualify this: the exercise 'does not, however, explain the differences in actual contributions from predicted contributions', which could reflect genuine savings responses or workers who previously contributed above their default rate continuing to do so. evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure illustrates how actual contribution rates to employer-sponsored retirement plans deviate from firm default contribution rates over time, for both the treatment and control groups. Firm default contribution rates are inferred as the median contribution rate among individuals working at the same firm, as described in Section VIC. Each panel A-D captures the distributions of deviations from firm default rates during a different year.

extraction_notes: 99 claims: one per RD coefficient the paper prints (Tables 2-7), plus the two descriptive distribution comparisons the paper draws conclusions from (Figures 4 and 9), the personal-plan contribution indicator reported only in the running text, and the two text-reported ratios of predicted to actual employer-plan responses.

Tables 2-7 carry no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals - only robust standard errors in parentheses. Where the paper states significance in prose (including blanket panel statements such as 'None of the estimates are statistically distinguishable from zero'), statistically_significant is transcribed from that statement. Where the paper is silent, it is computed as |estimate/SE| against 1.96 and a derivation evidence record records the arithmetic; those claims also carry an 'absent' record and an ambiguity note.
Page numbers everywhere are PDF page numbers (PDF page = printed journal page - 365), matching the convention the digest uses for figures.
Every quote was sliced verbatim out of the PDF text; spans crossing a hyphenated line break or containing a soft hyphen were avoided, which is why some quotes begin or end mid-sentence.

Table 4 column 4 prints the mean of the change in liabilities at age 63 as 3,269 without a minus sign, where every other liabilities mean in Tables 2-4 is negative; it is transcribed exactly as printed.
